# Installing a Real Application {.unnumbered} Third party software follows the same convention as the interpreter in [Install Apps](install-apps.qmd): its own directory tree under `/opt`, not scattered across the filesystem. Here's what that looks like for `baseball-trajectory`, a Shiny for Python app ([source](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/baseball-trajectory)) that plots a player's career arc from the MLB Stats API: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo git clone https://github.com/mjfrigaard/baseball-trajectory.git /opt/baseball-trajectory cd /opt/baseball-trajectory ``` ::: Create the virtual environment from the `/opt` Python (built in [Building Python from source](install-apps.qmd#building-python-from-source)), not the system one, then install the package and its dependencies into it: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -m venv /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv sudo /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/pip install -e . ``` ::: This pulls the app's dependencies from PyPI, so the instance needs outbound internet access. If the box is in a private subnet, verify the NAT gateway path works before you run this rather than after it hangs. The install spreads across three locations, and each one follows the convention from [Where do applications live?](install-apps.qmd#where-do-applications-live) rather than piling everything into one folder: | Location | What lives there | |:---------|:-----------------| | `/opt/baseball-trajectory` | Application source and the virtual environment | | `/etc/systemd/system/baseball-trajectory.service` | The unit file telling `systemd` how to run it | | `journald` | Application stdout and stderr, read with `journalctl -u baseball-trajectory` | : Where a system install of baseball-trajectory puts things {#tbl-baseball-trajectory-locations} ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'baseball-trajectory File Locations' %%| fig-width: 7.5 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"12px"}}}%% graph TD Root(["/"]) Opt("/opt/baseball-trajectory") Venv(".venv/bin/shiny
.venv/bin/baseball-trajectory") Etc("/etc/systemd/system") Unit("baseball-trajectory.service") Log("journald") Jctl("journalctl -u baseball-trajectory") Root --"application"--> Opt --> Venv Root --"config"--> Etc --> Unit Root --"logs"--> Log --> Jctl style Root fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Opt fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000,font-family:monospace style Venv fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000,font-family:monospace style Etc fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Unit fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Log fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace style Jctl fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff,font-family:monospace ``` Notice what's missing: there's no `/var/lib` entry. `baseball-trajectory` keeps nothing on disk. Rosters and career stats are fetched from `https://statsapi.mlb.com` and cached in memory, so a restart simply starts with an empty cache. That also means outbound HTTPS isn't just an install time requirement; the running app needs it on every new player lookup. Before handing it to `systemd`, confirm the console script starts from the venv: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/baseball-trajectory ``` ::: It binds to `127.0.0.1:8000`, so from a second SSH session `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000` should return `200 OK`. ## Daemonizing with `systemd` Now we turn `baseball-trajectory` into the kind of service described in [Lab 10](lab10.qmd), running under the service account from [Linux Users](linux-users.qmd). Started by hand from an SSH session, it dies the moment that session closes. When the app runs as a service, `systemd` starts it on boot, restarts it after a crash, and collects its output. In front of the app, nginx terminates TLS; [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) covers that setup. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'baseball-trajectory Deployment on EC2' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'look': 'classic', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"12px"}}}%% graph TD Op(["Operator
browser"]) Admin(["You
SSH client"]) subgraph EC2["EC2 Instance"] Nginx("nginx
:443 TLS") App("baseball-trajectory
127.0.0.1:8000") Sysd("systemd + journald") end MLB["MLB Stats API
statsapi.mlb.com"] Op --"HTTPS :443"--> Nginx Admin --"SSH :22"--> EC2 Nginx --"HTTP :8000"--> App App --"HTTPS :443"--> MLB Sysd --"supervises"--> App style EC2 fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Op fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Admin fill:#d2562b,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Nginx fill:#2a6f77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style App fill:#5b8c5a,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style MLB fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Sysd fill:#e8a33d,stroke:#000,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ``` Notice the one outbound arrow. The app pulls rosters and career stats from the MLB Stats API on demand, so the instance's security group and any NAT path have to allow outbound HTTPS, or the app starts cleanly and then fails on the first player lookup. Create the unit file: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/baseball-trajectory.service ``` ::: And give it this content: ```{.default} [Unit] Description=baseball-trajectory After=network.target [Service] Type=simple User=baseball-trajectory WorkingDirectory=/opt/baseball-trajectory ExecStart=/opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/shiny run baseball_trajectory.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target ``` Four directives control how the service runs: `User`, `ExecStart`, `--host`, and `Restart`. `User=baseball-trajectory` runs the process as the service account from [Linux Users](linux-users.qmd), not `root`. The app only serves requests and calls an external API, so that account needs no extra privilege at all. `ExecStart` uses the absolute path into the venv. There's no shell involved, no `PATH` to search, and no activation step. If this path is wrong the unit fails instantly, and it's the single most common cause of a failed first start. `--host 127.0.0.1` binds the app to loopback only. Change it to `0.0.0.0` and the app is reachable from the internet without TLS and without the proxy, which is exactly what we don't want. `Restart=on-failure` with `RestartSec=5` brings the app back after a crash, waiting five seconds between attempts so a fast crash loop doesn't spin the CPU. Load the new file and start the service: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now baseball-trajectory ``` ::: `daemon-reload` tells `systemd` to reread the unit files on disk. `enable` registers the unit to start on boot, and `--now` starts it immediately so you don't have to run `start` separately. ### Confirming it actually came up Never trust `enable --now` to mean the app is running. It means `systemd` tried. ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo systemctl status baseball-trajectory ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} ● baseball-trajectory.service - baseball-trajectory Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/baseball-trajectory.service; enabled; vendor preset: disabled) Active: active (running) since Sat 2026-09-05 18:22:41 UTC; 12s ago Main PID: 4812 (python3.12) CGroup: /system.slice/baseball-trajectory.service └─4812 /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/python3.12 /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/shiny run baseball_trajectory.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 Sep 05 18:22:41 ip-172-31-24-9 systemd[1]: Started baseball-trajectory. Sep 05 18:22:42 ip-172-31-24-9 shiny[4812]: INFO: Started server process [4812] Sep 05 18:22:42 ip-172-31-24-9 shiny[4812]: INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000 ``` ::: Two things to read here. `Active: active (running)` is the state, and `enabled` in the `Loaded:` line is the confirmation it will come back after a reboot. A unit can be running and not enabled, which works fine until the instance restarts. Then confirm something is actually listening, from the instance itself: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000 ``` ::: ::: {style="font-style: italic;"} ```{.default} HTTP/1.1 200 OK date: Sat, 05 Sep 2026 18:23:10 GMT server: uvicorn content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8 ``` ::: A `200` means the landing page rendered. A redirect is fine too. Connection refused means the process died between `status` and `curl`, and the journal will say why: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo journalctl -u baseball-trajectory -n 50 --no-pager ``` ::: `-u` filters to this unit, `-n 50` limits it to the last 50 lines, and `--no-pager` dumps it straight to the terminal instead of opening `less`. When you want to watch a start attempt live, `journalctl -u baseball-trajectory -f` follows the log the same way `tail -f` does. :::: {.callout-caution collapse='true' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Reading a failed start]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} Four failures account for almost every bad first start, and each has a distinct signature in `journalctl -u baseball-trajectory`: | What the journal says | What's actually wrong | |:----------------------|:----------------------| | `Failed at step EXEC ... No such file or directory` | The `ExecStart` path is wrong. Check it with `ls /opt/baseball-trajectory/.venv/bin/shiny` | | `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'baseball_trajectory'` | `pip install -e .` ran somewhere other than `/opt/baseball-trajectory`, or into a different venv | | `Address already in use` | Something already holds `:8000`, often a `shiny run` you started by hand and forgot | | `status=203/EXEC` with no other output | The venv was built from a Python that no longer exists at that path | The pattern in all four is the same: `systemd` executes a literal path with no shell, so anything the interactive session was quietly providing has to be spelled out in the unit file. ::: :::: ## Recap 1. A third party app gets its own tree under `/opt`: the source and a virtual environment built from the `/opt` Python, never the system copy. 2. The install spreads across three locations by purpose: the app under `/opt`, the unit file under `/etc/systemd/system`, and logs in `journald`. `baseball-trajectory` keeps no state on disk, so it has no `/var/lib` entry, but it needs outbound HTTPS at install time and at runtime. 3. Confirm the console script starts from the venv and answers on `127.0.0.1:8000` before handing it to `systemd`. 4. The `baseball-trajectory` unit runs as its own service account (`User=`), starts from an absolute `ExecStart` path into the venv, binds to `127.0.0.1` so only nginx can reach it, and restarts on failure. 5. After `systemctl enable --now`, confirm with `systemctl status` (`active (running)` and `enabled`) and `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8000`, and read `journalctl -u baseball-trajectory` when either one fails.
